source: Millidge, Tschantz, Buckley (2020) Whence the Expected Free Energy?
finding: Epistemic value is not a free consequence of extending free energy into the future. The natural 'free energy of the future' (FEF) has the epistemic term with the opposite sign and so punishes information seeking.
numbers: Algebraic result: epistemic term is positive in FEF and negative in EFE.
limits: Theory paper, no behavioural data.
agent_relevance: The explore drive in S3 must be put in on purpose. A scaffold does not get curiosity for free from 'minimise surprise'.

source: Millidge, Tschantz, Buckley (2020) Whence the Expected Free Energy?
finding: EFE equals FEF minus the expected information gain. So the curiosity term is an added piece. Authors offer a rival objective (FEEF) that keeps the epistemic term and is grounded as divergence between predicted and desired futures.
numbers: Algebraic result.
limits: FEEF is a proposal, not tested on behaviour here.
agent_relevance: Which objective is 'right' is open. Choose the explore rule for its use, not for its claimed derivation.

source: Millidge, Seth, Buckley (2021) Understanding the origin of information-seeking exploration in probabilistic objectives for control
finding: Splits objectives into evidence objectives (reward maximising, no built-in exploration) and divergence objectives (match expected to desired future, which split into an information-gain term). Argues divergence objectives explain probability matching as a feature rather than irrationality.
numbers: Theory; no sample.
limits: Probability-matching explanation is argued from the maths and tested only qualitatively. Read abstract, intro and objective decomposition.
agent_relevance: Pure reward-maximising prompts will not explore. A 'match the desired outcome distribution' framing can.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: In FrozenLake, active inference and Bayesian model-based RL behave almost the same once prior preferences are treated as rewards. In the stochastic version active inference scored far above the baselines.
numbers: Deterministic: AI 99.88 [99.64,100], Bayes RL 99.76, Q-learning (eps 0.1) 97.79. Stochastic: AI 98.90 [98.00,99.79] vs Bayes RL 64.39 and Q-learning about 65-66. 200 trials x 500 episodes.
limits: One tiny grid world. Authors say it is not representative. Stochastic gain is over weak baselines.
agent_relevance: Little support for 'curiosity beats RL' in general. Gains here come from having a belief model, not from the epistemic term itself.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: With no outcome preferences, the active inference agent has nothing to prefer and ends at goal or hole at random. With no reward at all, Q-learning stalls in a loop while belief-based agents keep exploring.
numbers: Null-preference AI scored 50.03 (det) and 50.22 (stoch). No-reward case: Q-learning 0.00 (15 moves), Bayes RL 39.94 (9.17 moves), AI 44.00 (8.67 moves).
limits: Same single environment. Information gain here is exploration for its own sake and fades once the world is known (stationary case).
agent_relevance: Epistemic value alone gives wandering, not purpose. Curiosity needs a goal and a stop rule.

source: Da Costa, Sajid, Parr, Friston, Smith (2023) Reward maximisation through discrete active inference
finding: Standard active inference gives Bellman-optimal (reward-maximising) actions only for a planning horizon of 1. Beyond that, recursive 'sophisticated' active inference is needed.
numbers: Formal proof: horizon 1 only for the standard scheme; any finite horizon for sophisticated inference.
limits: Proof covers discrete finite-horizon POMDPs only.
agent_relevance: A one-step 'most informative question now' rule is only myopically optimal. A real explore-exploit switch needs lookahead.

source: Da Costa, Sajid, Parr, Friston, Smith (2023) Reward maximisation through discrete active inference
finding: Directed exploration is said to emerge from risk and ambiguity terms in expected free energy, as against RL, which adds randomness or ad hoc information bonuses (UCB, Thompson sampling).
limits: A claim of the paper's discussion, shown by example rather than by comparison across many tasks.
agent_relevance: Both routes can be put into a prompt. The LLM studies below show the bonus route (summarised counts plus a hint) is what works today.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang, Slivkins (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama2 mostly fail to explore in multi-armed bandits. Only one configuration out of the tested set explored well: GPT-4 with a suggestive hint to explore, externally summarised per-arm averages, and zero-shot chain of thought.
numbers: 72 GPT-4 configs, 48 each for GPT-3.5 and Llama2; about 200K queries. Basic GPT-4 prompt: suffix failure in over 60% of replicates (5 arms, T=500). The winning config has suffix failure rate about 15% or less at T/2, like UCB and Thompson sampling.
limits: Simple bandits only. Authors note external summarising may be hard in complex tasks. GPT-4-0613 era.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence for our case: the explore state needs an explicit statistics table and an explicit instruction to explore.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang, Slivkins (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: Two failure modes. Suffix failure: the best arm is never chosen again after some round. Uniform-like failure: the model keeps picking all arms about equally and never narrows down. The same winning prompt without summarised history fails.
numbers: Distributional-output configs (BNRND, BSSCD) avoid suffix failure but show K x MinFrac not falling over time and lower reward (T=200, N=20).
limits: Surrogate statistics were built to detect failure with few replicates; they are proxies for long-run reward.
agent_relevance: Needs two guards: stop collapsing too early (suffix) and stop spreading forever (uniform). Both belong to the explore-to-exploit switch.

source: Nie, Su, Chang, Lee, Chi, Le, Chen (2025) EVOLvE: Evaluating and optimizing LLMs for exploration
finding: Gemma-2B/9B and Gemini-1.5 Flash/Pro fall short of UCB in bandits. Inference-time support with a summarised history or an algorithm-guided hint helps most, with no training.
numbers: Overall win-rate (MAB): Flash raw history 27.7, summarised 34.8, algorithm-guided 32.2; Pro raw 45.5, summarised 60.0, guided 59.6; UCB 90.6. Contextual bandit: Flash raw 0.0, guided 46.4; Pro raw 7.1, guided 64.3; LinUCB 96.4.
limits: Gemini and Gemma only; win-rate is by pairwise t-test over 30 trials per config.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that computes counts and a UCB-style bonus lifts a strong model by 15-60 points but still stays below the true algorithm.

source: Nie, Su, Chang, Lee, Chi, Le, Chen (2025) EVOLvE: Evaluating and optimizing LLMs for exploration
finding: Directed exploration in the model is weak: the share of pulls on the best arm barely rises for Flash. Few-shot demonstrations of good exploration help, and the best text format differs by method.
numbers: Flash best-arm fraction 9.3 to 10.7 while UCB 32.7 to 65.0. Few-shot, Flash: raw history 27.5 vs algorithm-guided 50.2. Fine-tuned Flash: raw 65.6 vs summarised 28.3. Hard-task training 65.6 vs easy 54.5.
limits: Fine-tuning is not open to a scaffold-only agent.
agent_relevance: Few-shot examples of 'good exploration traces' in summarised form are a usable scaffold piece.

source: Monea, Bosselut, Brantley, Artzi (2025) LLMs are in-context bandit reinforcement learners
finding: LLMs learn from reward feedback in context only when enough randomness is present. Keeping only positive-reward episodes works best. Randomly subsampling past episodes (Stochastic ICRL) raises exploration and stabilises learning better than raising temperature.
numbers: Qwen2.5 sizes 0.5B to 72B; performance correlates strongly with scale. Performance often dips suddenly then recovers with naive version. Exact accuracies not recorded.
limits: Classification-as-bandit tasks, not open-ended work. Naive version cannot use negative signals well.
agent_relevance: Showing a random subset of past attempts is a cheap exploration source for the scaffold.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: On the Horizon task GPT-3 matched humans at short horizon and had lower overall regret, but showed no directed exploration and did not scale its noise with horizon.
numbers: Overall regret GPT-3 M=2.72 (SD 5.98) vs humans 3.24 (SD 10.26), t(38878)=-5.03, p<.001. Short horizon: t(5566)=-0.043, p=.97. Horizon effect on picking the informative option beta=-0.15, z=-0.56, p=.58. Horizon x value interaction beta=-0.02, p=.14.
limits: text-davinci at temperature 0, 2022. Newer models and chain of thought not tested here.
agent_relevance: A base LLM ignores how many decisions remain. The scaffold must state the horizon and act on it.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 showed some value-based random exploration, and a bias to repeat the option it had seen more, which the authors link to next-word prediction.
numbers: Value effect beta=0.18 (SE 0.01), z=14.48, p<.001.
limits: Humans also show perseveration in other tasks, but the horizon process overrides it in this task.
agent_relevance: Repeating what is already in context is a default; an explore step must push against it.

source: Coda-Forno, Binz, Akata et al. (2023) Meta-in-context learning in large language models
finding: In two-armed bandits GPT-3 improves as it sees more tasks in context. Its prior expectations shift toward the true reward distribution and it becomes greedier. It avoids uncertain options by default.
numbers: Matched a greedy policy after about 4 tasks, slightly behind UCB. In-context beta=-0.221, t=-35.8; meta effect beta=-0.031, t=-5.0. Prior mean 545.22 (SD 6359) before vs 6.49 (SD 4.41) after. Relative uncertainty beta=-0.160 (z=-31.8); UCB use rose only +0.046.
limits: GPT-3, simple bandits. Gains come from prior calibration and exploiting, not from more curiosity.
agent_relevance: Calibrating the starting prior may matter more than boosting curiosity. Uncertainty aversion is the default and needs overriding.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: uncertainty-aware planning enhances information seeking in LLMs
finding: Scoring candidate questions by expected information gain (simulate answers, compute entropy reduction, propagate over a tree) raises success in 20 Questions, diagnosis and troubleshooting. This is an LLM version of epistemic value.
numbers: Average success gain 38.1% over direct prompting. Llama3-70B closed-set: 20Q-Things 15.0 -> 25.0, DX 83.7 -> 90.4, MedDG 60.2 -> 64.3, FloDial 28.8 -> 47.1. GPT-4 troubleshooting 43.7 -> 67.3.
limits: Closed hypothesis set works best; open set gains are smaller (UoT open-set beats adapted-ToT by 8.7%). Answerer is also an LLM. No clean ablation of information gain versus tree search recorded here.
agent_relevance: Template for an S3 operator: propose questions, simulate each answer, pick the one that splits the hypotheses most evenly.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: uncertainty-aware planning enhances information seeking in LLMs
finding: Gains are larger for weaker open-set settings and shorten conversations: fewer turns to reach the answer.
numbers: Llama3-70B DX closed-set: mean successful length 3.5 -> 1.0 turns; MedDG 3.5 -> 1.4. Mistral-Large 20Q-Common closed-set 26.1 -> 31.5.
limits: Small gains on hard 20-Question sets for weaker models (Mistral 20Q-Things open 12.5 -> 15.0).
agent_relevance: Information-gain questioning cuts cost as well as raising accuracy: a ready stop rule is 'ask until one hypothesis dominates'.

source: Schwartenbeck, Passecker, Hauser, FitzGerald, Kronbichler, Friston (2019) Computational mechanisms of curiosity and goal-directed exploration
finding: Two kinds of epistemic value: hidden-state exploration (seek unambiguous observations to know the current state) and model-parameter exploration (seek novel, uncertain options to learn the task). They can conflict.
numbers: Simulations of a two-armed bandit with a risky and a safe option; no human subjects.
limits: Simulation only; behavioural predictions were not tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: Separate 'find out what the state is' (diagnose) from 'find out how the task works' (learn). Different triggers, different stop rules.

source: Schwartenbeck, Passecker, Hauser, FitzGerald, Kronbichler, Friston (2019) Computational mechanisms of curiosity and goal-directed exploration
finding: Random exploration becomes adaptive only when directed uncertainty reduction fails or is impossible. Active learning needs stable regularities across trials; active inference suits trial-by-trial change.
limits: Argument from simulations and discussion.
agent_relevance: If the scaffold cannot compute what a probe would tell it, fall back to diversified sampling.

source: Wilson, Geana, White, Ludvig, Cohen (2014) Humans use directed and random exploration to solve the explore-exploit dilemma
finding: Horizon task: with 6 free choices left, people seek information more (directed) and choose more noisily (random) than with 1 choice left.
numbers: N=30 analysed (31 recruited, mean age 19.7, Princeton); 320 games. Information bonus up: t(29)=5.05, p<1e-4, 25 of 30. Decision noise up: F(1,119)=65.97, p<1e-8, 28 of 30.
limits: Small student sample. Read via a fetch summary of the full text, not the PDF.
agent_relevance: Human benchmark: more steps left means more exploring. Set an exploration budget from steps remaining.

source: Wilson, Geana, White, Ludvig, Cohen (2014) Humans use directed and random exploration to solve the explore-exploit dilemma
finding: The measured information bonus was larger than the optimal model's value and the noise is not optimal. No difference between horizon 6 and 11.
numbers: Supplement: horizons 1, 6, 11; no 6 vs 11 difference. Reward independent of information on first free choice: F(2,89)=0.09, p=.91.
limits: Only two horizons in the main study. Reward and information confounded after the first free choice. Ambiguity preference may distort estimates.
agent_relevance: Humans over-explore against the optimum; do not copy human levels as a target.

source: Zajkowski, Kossut, Wilson (2017) A causal role for right frontopolar cortex in directed, but not random, exploration
finding: TMS over right frontopolar cortex reduced directed exploration and left random exploration intact.
limits: Abstract only; effect size not recorded.
agent_relevance: Directed and random exploration are separable, so a scaffold can tune them apart.

source: Gershman (2018) Deconstructing the human algorithms for exploration
finding: Uncertainty-bonus algorithms predict a bias shift; sampling algorithms predict a slope change. Two experiments showed both and a hybrid model fit best.
limits: Abstract only. A rival to the pure two-strategy account.
agent_relevance: Rival to a single information-gain term. A bonus plus sampling mix is the better human account; Coda-Forno 2023 reused this fit on GPT-3.

source: Sadeghiyeh, Wang, Hallquist, Wilson et al. (2020) Temporal discounting correlates with directed exploration but not with random exploration
finding: More temporal discounting goes with less directed exploration; no link with random exploration. The link seems driven by uncertainty seeking.
limits: Abstract only; correlation size not recorded.
agent_relevance: Moderator: impatience cuts directed exploration. In an agent a short budget should cut information seeking.

source: Somerville et al. (2017) Charting the expansion of strategic exploratory behavior during adolescence
finding: Strategic directed exploration (more information seeking at long horizons) emerged during adolescence and then held steady. Strategic random exploration was similar across ages.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Directed exploration is a developed, horizon-sensitive skill; this matches the LLM pattern in Binz & Schulz.

source: Wilson, Bonawitz, Costa, Ebitz (2021) Balancing exploration and exploitation with information and randomization
finding: Review: many organisms use an information bias and choice randomisation, with different neural and lifespan profiles.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: The two-strategy split is the field consensus as of 2021, with Gershman's hybrid as the main challenge.

source: Friston, Rigoli, Ognibene, Mathys, FitzGerald, Pezzulo (2015) Active inference and epistemic value
finding: Founding paper: expected free energy contains epistemic value (expected information gain) and extrinsic value (reward). Not opened this session.
limits: Not read; no numbers. Disputed by Millidge et al. 2020 on whether the epistemic term follows from the principle.
agent_relevance: Origin of the rule: explore while expected information gain exceeds what preferred outcomes offer.

source: Friston, Lin, Frith, Pezzulo, Hobson, Ondobaka (2017) Active inference, curiosity and insight
finding: Founding paper linking curiosity and insight to active inference. Not opened this session.
limits: Not read; no numbers.
agent_relevance: Still unconfirmed by an opened source; keep as a hypothesis in the schema.
